children.title: Trying to enrol and vote
children.description: There are a number of barriers or issues that can get between people and enrolling and voting - which of these apply?

children.title: Working or child care gets in the way of voting
children.description: Working or child care gets in the way

children.title: I have to bring my kids with me
children.question: I am a parent with young children and I have no one to watch them while I vote. Am I allowed to bring my children with me when I vote?
children.vote: The law requires a person to enter the voting booth alone, which is intended to protect the secrecy of their vote. However, in practice, you may take your children into the voting booth with you if they cannot be left unattended.

children.title: I am an essential worker / working on election day
children.question: I'm an essential worker who is working on election day, can I leave work to vote?
children.vote:
You are legally entitled to time away from work to vote on election day. You can also vote early at an [[advance-voting]] place. 

If you have not had a reasonable opportunity to vote before starting work on election day, and you are not required to carry out essential work or services, your employer must allow you to leave work to vote by 3pm. You are entitled to remain away from work for the rest of the day if necessary to vote, and your employer cannot deduct pay for the time off you take to vote. 

If you are required to work after 3pm to carry out essential work or services, your employer must allow you a reasonable amount of time earlier in the day to vote. Your employer cannot deduct pay for this time, provided you do not take more than two hours off work.

children.title: I am living somewhere temporarily for work e.g. seasonal workers, sharemilkers, away at training
children.question: I am doing seasonal farming work during the election period. Can I still vote away from my usual address?
children.enrol: You can enrol online or by completing a paper form. Your residential address for enrolment purposes does not change if you are temporarily away from your usual home.
children.vote: If you are away from your usual place of residence, you can vote at the nearest voting place. As your name will not appear on the printed electoral roll at that location, you will need to complete a special declaration vote form before voting. This is known as a [[special-vote]].
source: Electoral Act s 61(b), s 72(6)(a), and s 162.

children.title: I am a shift worker
children.question: I work night shifts and sleep during the day, how can I cast my vote?
children.vote: You can either vote during the [[advance-voting]] period or cast a [[takeaway-vote]].

children.title: I can't physically get to a polling place
I will be/am currently in hospital
children.question: I have to get surgery on the Friday before polling day, how do I vote?
children.enrol: You can enrol online or by completing a paper form, and you can have someone support you with the process if needed. Your enrolment address should be your usual residential address, not the hospital where you will be staying.
children.vote:
If you cannot get to a voting place because you are in hospital, you can authorise a friend or family member to collect your voting papers and bring them to you so you can cast a [[takeaway-vote]]. 

If you are scheduled to go into hospital before election day, it is best to vote in advance if you can. [[Advance-voting]] begins on **26 October**, 12 days before election day.

children.title: I can't leave care/ or the house
children.question: I have health issues and do not like being in public, crowded, spaces. Can I still vote?
children.vote:
You can authorise someone to collect your voting papers from a voting place on your behalf - this process is known as a [[takeaway-vote]]. 

If you cannot get to a voting place and do not have someone who can collect your voting papers for you, contact your electorate manager. It may be possible for your voting papers to be delivered to you and then collected once you have completed them.

children.title: I am on home detention
children.question: I am serving a 6 month home detention sentence, can I still enrol to vote?
children.enrol: If you are on home detention, you can still enrol to vote, provided you meet the general eligibility criteria. You can enrol online or by completing a paper form.
children.vote: You can vote if you are on home detention or serving a community-based sentence. Election officials will provide your local probation services office with information about the voting options available to you.

children.title: I am in a rest home
children.question: I live in a residential care facility and can't enrol or vote on my own, I have no family to help me with this, how can I vote?
children.vote: If you are in a rest home and you won’t be able to go to a voting place, you don’t need to contact the Electoral Commission. Your local electorate manager will contact the manager of your care home to arrange voting services.

children.title: I have a physical disability
children.question: I have lost a lot of motor functions, including the use of my hands… can I vote? How do I seek assistance to vote?
children.enrol:
You can ask someone, such as a friend or family member, to support you in completing your enrolment form or to complete it on your behalf. 

A person who is enrolled to vote can complete and sign the form for you, and someone with power of attorney can also complete and sign it on your behalf. 

You can enrol online, or upload, email or post a completed form.
children.vote:
You can authorise someone to collect your voting papers from a voting place and bring them to you - this process is known as a [[takeaway-vote]].  

If you cannot get to a voting place and do not have someone who can collect your voting papers, contact your electorate manager. It may be possible for your voting papers to be delivered to you and then collected once you have completed them. 

You can also cast your vote at an [[advance-voting]] place and bring a support person with you, including behind the voting screen if you would like.
source: Electoral Act s 170, s 167(2A), and s 85.

children.title: Names and identity
I have no ID
children.question: I don't have a license, passport, or kiwi access card, can I still enrol and vote without any of these?
children.enrol:
To enrol *online*, you need a **New Zealand drivers licence**, **New Zealand passport**, or a **verified RealMe identity**. 

If you do not have any of these, you can still enrol by completing an enrolment form online and having it emailed to you to sign, then uploading, emailing or posting the completed form. 

Alternatively, you can print a form yourself or request one to be sent to you, then return it by upload, email or post. Printed enrolment forms may also be available at selected public libraries, Electoral Commission offices, and potentially local post offices. Contact your local library or post office for more information.
children.vote: You do not need to bring any form of ID to vote. Simply turn up at a voting place. You can bring your EasyVote card to make the process quicker, but if you do not have one, that is okay too. Your details can be confirmed at the voting place.

children.title: I am gender diverse and have changed my name
children.question: My prefered name differs from my legal name, and has not been legally changed from my birth name. I am concerned about being questioned in public when I go to vote. What can I do?
children.enrol:
While the Electoral Act requires your 'full' name to be used for voting and enrolment purposes, the Electoral Comissions does allow preferred names to be used (this does not have to match a legal record). 

If you are already enrolled but would like to change your enrolment details to match your preferred name, and this name vastly differs from the name that your are currently enrolled under, please ensure that you include the previously enrolled name when you are updating your details e.g., (previously enrolled as *Full name*) - this is to avoid potential issues regarding duplicate records. 

Please note, you may be limited when trying to use the online enrolment service, as it uses the details from your New Zealand passport, drivers licence or verified RealMe identity. If your preferred name does not match these records, you may need to complete a paper enrolment form instead and then upload, email or post it to the Electoral Commission. You may be contacted by the Electoral Comission to double check these details.
children.vote: You can vote using your preferred name if you were able to update your details before the enrolment due date on **25 October**.

children.title: I have made a change to my legal name e.g. through marriage, divorce, adoption, or reclaiming an ingoa Māori
children.question: I no longer identify with my ex-husbands surname. Can I vote with my maiden name, despite not legally changing my name on my ID?
children.enrol:
While the Electoral Act requires your 'full' name to be used for voting and enrolment purposes, the Electoral Comissions does allow preferred names to be used (this does not have to match a legal record). 

If you are already enrolled but would like to change your enrolment details to match your preferred name, and this name vastly differs from the name that your are currently enrolled under, please ensure that you include this name when you are updating your details e.g., (previously enrolled as *Full name*) - this is to avoid potential issues regarding duplicate records. 

Please note, you may be limited when trying to use the online enrolment service, as it uses the details from your New Zealand passport, drivers licence or verified RealMe identity. If your preferred name does not match these records, you may need to complete a paper enrolment form instead and then upload, email or post it to the Electoral Commission. You may be contacted by the Electoral Comission to double check these details.
children.vote: You can vote using your preferred name if you were able to update your details before the enrolment due date on **25 October**.

children.title: Age
I am 17 but will turn 18 on or before the election day
children.question: I am currently 17 years old and won't turn 18 until the day before election. Can I still enrol to vote?
children.enrol: You can complete an enrolment form when you are 17. On your 18th birthday, you will be automatically enrolled and able to vote.
children.vote: If you turn 18 on election day, you can still vote as normal, provided you enrolled beforehand. If you enrolled **before 4 October**, you can cast an [[election-day-vote]]. If you enrolled **after 4 October but before 25 October**, you will cast a [[special-vote]] at the voting place.

children.title: I don't have a normal, fixed address
I live in a remote area
children.question: I'll be in a remote area during the election with no voting places near me, how can I cast a vote?
children.vote:
You can authorise someone to collect your voting papers from a voting place on your behalf. If you cannot get to a voting place and do not have someone who can collect your voting papers, contact your electorate manager. 

They may be able to arrange for your voting papers to be delivered to you and then collected once you have completed them. If you are in a remote location within Aotearoa New Zealand, you may also be able to cast a [[special-vote]] if voting at a polling place would not be practicable without causing hardship or serious inconvenience. 

If you are unable to reach a voting place because you are in a remote location—for example, on a remote island administered by the Department of Conservation, at an offshore installation, or working on a vessel during the voting period—the Electoral Commission has a separate process for arranging voting services. For more information, call 0800 36 76 56.

children.title: I work at sea
children.question: I work on a cruise ship and will be working away from port during election time, how can I enrol and vote?
children.enrol: Your residential address for enrolment purposes does not change if you are temporarily absent from it.
children.vote:
If you are working on a ship that is in port and you are enrolled, or eligible to enrol, in the electorate where the ship is located, your ship’s master must allow you to go ashore to vote. If the ship will not be in port, or will not return to port, during the voting period, you may be eligible for a [[special-vote]]. 

For help with enrolling and voting, contact the Electoral Commission closer to election time on 0800 36 76 56 or at <enquiries@elections.govt.nz>.

children.title: I live on a boat
children.question: For the past few years, I have been living full-time on a boat. Can I enrol to vote?
children.enrol: If your home is on a ship or boat that is permanently moored in a harbour, use the address of the ship or boat as your residential address. If your home is on a travelling ship or boat, use the last New Zealand address where you lived for at least 1 month, even if this was some time ago. You will also need to provide a postal address where you can receive mail, such as a PO Box or the address of a friend, family member, church or support group.

children.title: I do not have stable housing or a normal address
children.question: I am experiencing homelessness/am unhoused and do no have an address to enrol, how can I still complete my enrolment form?
children.enrol:
You can enrol at a place where you spend a lot of time, or use your last residential address where you lived for at least 1 month, even if this was some time ago. 

If you do not feel safe receiving mail at this address, you can provide a different *postal* address where you can safely receive correspondence, such as the address of a friend, family member, church or support group.
children.vote:
The Electoral Commission lists all voting places online, so you can find one near you, or you can call 0800 36 76 56 for assistance. Voting places are often located at community hubs. 

To vote, simply go to a voting place during the [[advance-voting]] period from **26 October to 6 October** or on election day on **7 October**. The voting team will support you through the process, and you do not need to bring any form of ID.

children.title: I live overseas and do not have a New Zealand address
children.question: I am a kiwi who has recently moved overseas and do not have a New Zealand address, can I still vote?
children.enrol:
If you are a New Zealand citizen who has lived in New Zealand continuously for more than 12 months at some point in your life and have been in New Zealand within the last 3 years, you are still eligible to enrol to vote. 

Not having a current New Zealand address does not prevent you from enrolling. Your electorate will be based on the last New Zealand address where you lived for at least **1 month**, and you can use your overseas address as your *postal* address to receive correspondence. 

You can enrol online using a **New Zealand passport**, **New Zealand drivers licence** or **verified RealMe identity**. If you do not have any of these, you can enrol using a paper form.
children.vote:
If you are overseas, you can download your voting papers from the Electoral Commission’s website, complete them and upload them online (you cannot return voting papers by email).

A link to download your voting papers will be available when overseas voting opens on **21 October**. You can complete the papers digitally or by hand. If completing them by hand, you can scan and upload them online, or post or hand-deliver them to an overseas voting place. 

If uploading your voting papers, they must be received by **7pm (NZ time)** on election day, which is **7 November**. 

You may also be able to vote in person at an overseas voting place. A list of overseas voting places will be available on the Electoral Commission’s website before the election.

children.title: Enrolment issues
I have been placed on the dormant roll
children.question: I haven't voted in a while. I have tried to enrol but found I have been placed on the dormant roll. How do I vote?
children.enrol:
To come off the [[dormant-roll]], you simply need to update your enrolment address. You must do this before voting starts on **26 October 2026**, as you cannot update your enrolment details at a voting place. 

To check or update your enrolment details, visit vote.nz or call 0800 36 76 56.
children.vote:
If you update your enrolment address before enrolment closes, you can vote normally. 

If you do not update your address **before midnight on 25 October** and have been on the dormant roll for less than 3 years, you can still vote. 

If your current address is in the same electorate as your previous enrolment address, you can cast both a party vote and an electorate vote. However, if your current address is in a different electorate, you can only cast a party vote.

children.title: My enrolment details have changed
children.question: I have moved address recently, how do I change my enrolment information?
children.enrol:
You can enrol, check or update your details online at vote.nz using your **New Zealand drivers licence**, **New Zealand passport** or **verified RealMe identity**. 

You can also call 0800 36 76 56 to request an enrolment form, or free-text your name and address to 3676 to have a form sent to you. 

Providing your email address, phone number and postal address to the Electoral Commission will help them keep you updated about enrolment and voting.

children.title: I want to be on the unpublished roll
children.question: I worry that my abusive ex partner will find my new confidential address if I enrol to vote. Can I enrol to vote without my information becoming publicly accessible?
children.enrol:
You can apply to be on the [[unpublished-roll]], which means your details will not appear on publicly available printed electoral rolls. 

To apply, you can download and complete an application form and email it to the Electoral Commission, or call 0800 36 76 56 to have a form sent to you by post. 

You will need to provide evidence explaining why you need to be on the unpublished roll, such as a letter from your employer, lawyer, social worker, advocate or another person of standing in the community explaining why your circumstances place you at risk. 

You can also provide documents such as a current protection order under the Family Violence Act 2018 or a restraining order under the Harassment Act 1997.
children.vote: You can vote at any voting place in a general election, referendum or by-election. You will need to cast a [[special-vote]] because your details will not appear on the printed electoral roll used to issue voting papers at the voting place.

children.title: Health and disability
I will be/am currently in the hospital
children.question: I have to get surgery on the Friday before polling day, how do I vote?
children.enrol: You can enrol online or by completing a paper form, and you can have someone support you with the process if needed. Your enrolment address should be your usual residential address, not the hospital where you will be staying.
children.vote:
If you cannot get to a voting place because you are in hospital, you can authorise a friend or family member to collect your voting papers and bring them to you so you can cast a [[takeaway-vote]]. If you are scheduled to go into hospital before election day, it is best to vote in advance if you can. 

[[Advance-voting]] begins on **26 October**, 12 days before election day.

children.title: I am sectioned under the Mental Health Act
children.question: I've been detained in a hospital or secure facility for more than 3 years, can I still enrol and vote?
children.enrol:
If you’ve been detained in a hospital or secure facility for 3 years or less, you can enrol and vote, as long as you meet the general eligibility requirements for enrolment.

If you’ve been detained in a hospital or secure facility, or you’re subject to a compulsory treatment order, for more than 3 years, under:

- Section 24, or section 31 or section 33 of the Criminal Procedure (Mentally Impaired Persons) Act 2003, or under the corresponding provisions of the Criminal Justice Act 1985 (having been found unfit to stand trial or acquitted on account of insanity)
- Section 34 of the Criminal Procedure (Mentally Impaired Persons) Act 2003 or section 118 of the Criminal Justice Act 1985 (following conviction for an offence)
- Section 45(2) of the Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992 (the Mental Health Act), or section 29(1) of the Intellectual Disability (Compulsory Care and Rehabilitation) Act 2003 (for treatment of persons otherwise detained in prison because of their mental health or intellectual disability)

then you are *ineligible* to enrol and vote while you’re detained.

The Director of Mental Health (or their delegate) is required to inform the Electoral Commission of any person detained in a hospital or secure facility who is, or becomes, ineligible to vote. The Electoral Commission will then remove them from the electoral roll.

When a person detained in a hospital or secure facility has been transferred from a prison or is released from the facility (as long as they are not released to prison), the Director of Mental Health is required to provide them with the opportunity to enrol to vote, if they are eligible. If they choose to exercise that opportunity, the Director of Mental Health must pass their enrolment information to the Electoral Commission.
children.vote:
If you have been detained for 3 years or less as at election day you can enrol to vote if you also meet the general eligibility requirements. 

If you are eligible to vote from your facility, you’ll be able to participate in the 2026 General Election if you choose to. The Electoral Commission will work with your facility to provide you with voting services.
source:
- Section 24, or section 31 or section 33 of the Criminal Procedure (Mentally Impaired Persons) Act 2003, or under the corresponding provisions of the Criminal Justice Act 1985 (having been found unfit to stand trial or acquitted on account of insanity)
- Section 34 of the Criminal Procedure (Mentally Impaired Persons) Act 2003 or section 118 of the Criminal Justice Act 1985 (following conviction for an offence)
- Section 45(2) of the Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992 (the Mental Health Act), or section 29(1) of the Intellectual Disability (Compulsory Care and Rehabilitation) Act 2003 (for treatment of persons otherwise detained in prison because of their mental health or intellectual disability)

children.title: I am blind or have low vision
children.question: I am partially blind and need help reading and marking the paper to vote, how can I receive help?
children.enrol:
A support person can help you enrol online or via paper form if you're blind or have low vision. 

If you can't sign the form, a support person can complete the form on your behalf.
children.vote:
You may bring a support person to assist you to help you vote, read out the voting paper, and mark the paper for you if necessary. 

Furthermore, a telephone dictation voting service is available for blind and vision-impaired voters and voters who have a physical disability that prevents them from marking the voting paper independently and in secret. 

You need to register to use this service, even if you've used it at previous elections.

**Registration** for the telephone dictation service opens on **Monday 5 October 2026**, and will close at **noon** (NZT) on election day, **Saturday 7 November 2026**.

**Voting** with the telephone dictation service opens on **Wednesday 21 October 2026**, and will close at **7pm** (NZT) on election day, **Saturday 7 November 2026**.

children.title: I have a physical disability
children.question: I have lost a lot of motor functions, including the use of my hands… can I vote? How do I seek assistance to vote?
children.enrol:
You can ask someone, such as a friend or family member, to support you in completing your enrolment form or to complete it on your behalf. 

A person who is enrolled to vote can complete and sign the form for you, and someone with power of attorney can also complete and sign it on your behalf. 

You can enrol online, or upload, email or post a completed form.
children.vote:
You can authorise someone to collect your voting papers from a voting place and bring them to you. This is known as a [[takeaway-vote]]. 

If you cannot get to a voting place and do not have someone who can collect your voting papers, contact your electorate manager. It may be possible for your voting papers to be delivered to you and then collected once you have completed them. 

You can also cast a vote in the [[advance-voting]] period and bring a support person with you to the voting place, including behind the voting screen if you would like.
source: Electoral Act s 170, s 167(2A), and s 85.

children.title: I have a mental health issue
children.question: I struggle with severe anxiety and don't know if I can vote on my own, how can I get help to enrol and vote?
children.enrol:
You can ask a support person to help you enrol online if you wish. 

A support person can also complete and sign an enrolment form on your behalf if you require help because of a mental impairment. 

To *sign* the enrolment form on your behalf, the support person must be enrolled to vote; have enduring power of attorney; or be the person’s appointed welfare guardian. If required, the support person can also fill in another form so the Electoral Commission can contact them as your representative.
children.vote:
If you need help with voting, a friend, family member or electoral official can be your support person and assist you.

Your support person can:

- Go behind the voting screen with you
- Read out the words and information on your voting paper
- Mark the voting papers for you if you ask them to.
- Your support person can't tell you who you should vote for. 

You can vote as long as you want to and can clearly indicate your voting choice. However, you must be present and able to indicate you choice at the time the vote is cast. If you're not able to do this, no one can cast a vote on your behalf, even someone with power of attorney or guardianship.

children.title: I have dementia or am helping someone with dementia
children.question: My grandparent has dementia, can they still vote?
children.enrol:
A support person can help someone with dementia to enrol to vote. A support person can also complete and sign an enrolment form on their behalf if they require help. 

To *sign* the enrolment form on their behalf, the support person must be enrolled to vote; have enduring power of attorney; or be the person’s appointed welfare guardian. 

If you're helping someone with dementia enrol, you will need to fill in another form so the Electoral Commission can contact you as their representative. Ring 0800 36 76 56 for the form.
children.vote:
People living with dementia, or any other cognitive impairment, are able to continue to vote if they wish to do so. They can have help voting by taking a support person with them to the voting place.

A person with dementia can vote as long as they want to and can clearly indicate their voting choice. However, they must be present and able to indicate their choice at the time the vote is cast. If they're not able to do this, no one can cast a vote on their behalf, even someone with power of attorney or guardianship.

children.title: I need help marking the paper
children.question: I struggle with gripping pens/pencils to write and need help marking the voting papers
children.vote:
You may bring a support person to assist you, they can help you vote, read out the voting paper and mark the paper for you if necessary. 

Your support person cannot tell you who to vote for.

children.title: Prison, remand, home detention etc
I am on home detention
children.question: I am serving a 6 month home detention sentence, how can I my vote if I can't leave home?
children.enrol: If you are on home detention, you can still enrol to vote, provided you meet the general eligibility criteria. You can enrol online or by completing a paper form.
children.vote: You can vote if you are on home detention or serving a community-based sentence. Election officials will provide your local Probation Services office with information about the voting options available to you.

children.title: I am in prison
children.question: I am currently serving a prison sentence of 2 years, can I still vote and will I be able to vote from prison?
children.enrol: You can still enrol, but this depends on when the offences you were sentenced for occured. If the offences you were sentenced for were before 20 December 2025 and your sentence is under 3 years, you can enrol and vote. Prison staff assist those who are eligible and enrolment applications are individually scanned and emailed to the Electoral Commission.
children.vote:
This depends on when the offences you were sentenced for occured. If the offences you were sentenced for were before 20 December 2025 and your sentence is under 3 years, you can vote. 

During the [[advance-voting]] period, mobile voting teams will attend prisons and set up voting facilities for prisoners who are eligible to vote.

children.title: I am on remand
children.question: I'm in prison while on remand waiting for my trial, can I still enrol to vote?
children.enrol: If you're on remand, you can still enrol to vote if you meet the general eligibility criteria. You do not face the same restrictions as those who have been sentenced. If you are in prison while on remand, prison staff will assist those who are eligible and enrolment applications are individually scanned and emailed to the Electoral Commission.
children.vote: If you're in a police cell in the electorate on election day, a voting team may visit before midday so you can vote. If you are in prison while on remand, during the [[advance-voting]] period, mobile voting teams will attend prisons and set up voting facilities for those who are eligible to vote.

children.title: I am on community service
children.question: I'm serving a community service sentence can I still vote?
children.enrol: If you're serving a community based sentence, you can still enrol to vote. You can do this online or via paper form.
children.vote: You can vote if you're on home detention or serving a community-based sentence. Election officials will give your local Probation Services information about the voting options available to you.

children.title: Overseas voters
I am living overseas
children.question: I am living or staying in Australia at the time of the election, can I still enrol and vote and how can I do it?
children.enrol:
If you are a New Zealand citizen, who has lived in New Zealand for more than 12 months continuously at some point in your life **AND** have been to New Zealand in the last 3 years - you are still eligible to enrol to vote. Your electorate will be where you last lived in New Zealand for longer than 1 month and you may set your postal address to your overseas address to ensure you receive correspondence. 

You can enrol online using a **New Zealand passport** or a **New Zealand drivers licence** or a **verified Realme login**. If you don't have either of these, you can also enrol via paper form.
children.vote:
You can cast a [[special-vote]].

The best way to vote from overseas is to download your voting papers from the electoral commission's website, complete them, then upload them online (you cannot send back voting papers through email). 

A link to download your voting papers will be available on the electoral commission's website from the date overseas voting opens on **21 October**. You can complete the papers both digitally (marking the paper digitally) or physically, if you choose to complete them by hand you can scan and upload them online, or you can post or hand deliver them to your nearest overseas voting place. 

If you're uploading your voting papers, you must return them by **7pm (NZ time)** on election day which is **7 November**.

You may also be able to vote at an overseas voting place. A list of overseas voting places will be available on the electoral commission's website prior to the election.

children.title: I am overseas as a member of the military or diplomatic service
children.question: I am a member of the New Zealand Defence Force and stationed overseas, can I still enrol to vote?
children.enrol:
You can enrol and vote no matter how long you've been outside of New Zealand if you are one of the following: public servant working overseas and their families; New Zealand diplomats or trade representatives and their families; members of the New Zealand Defence Force and their families. 

You can enrol online using a **New Zealand passport** or a **New Zealand drivers licence** or a **verified Realme login**. If you don't have either of these, you can also enrol via paper form.
children.vote:
You can cast a [[special-vote]].
The best way to vote from overseas is to download your voting papers from the electoral commission’s website, complete them, then upload them (you cannot send back voting papers through email). 

A link to download your voting papers will be available on the electoral commission's website from the date overseas voting opens on **21 October**. You can complete the papers both digitally or physically, if you choose to complete them by hand you can scan and upload them online, or you can post or hand deliver them to your nearest overseas voting place. 

If you're uploading your voting papers, you must return them by **7pm (NZ time)** on election day which is **7 November**.

children.title: I am a seasonal worker or temporarily living overseas for work
children.question: I am living somewhere temporarily for work for a few months, how do I vote?
children.enrol:
You can still enrol and vote if you are a New Zealand citizen or resident for electoral purposes and only residing outside of New Zealand temporarily for work (if you have been back to New Zealand in the last 3 years). Your residential address for enrolment purposes does not change because you are temporarily absent from it. 

You can enrol online using a **New Zealand passport** or a **New Zealand drivers licence** or a **verified Realme login**. If you don't have either of these, you can also enrol via paper form.
children.vote:
You can cast a [[special-vote]].

The best way to vote from overseas is to download your voting papers from the electoral commission’s website, complete them, then upload them (you cannot send back voting papers through email). 

A link to download your voting papers will be available on the electoral commission's website from the date overseas voting opens on **21 October**. You can complete the papers both digitally or physically, if you choose to complete them by hand you can scan and upload them online, or you can post or hand deliver them to your nearest overseas voting place.

If you're uploading your voting papers, you must return them by **7pm (NZ time)** on election day which is **7 November**.

children.title: Migrant in NZ, residents & language
I have migrated to New Zealand / I am a resident or visa holder
children.question: I am a migrant in NZ who has been here for 2 years and I have never voted before, am I able to vote?
children.enrol:
You can enrol to vote as a migrant, resident or visa holder **IF** you have a visa that does not require you to leave within a specified time **AND** you must have lived in New Zealand continuously for 12 months or more (this generally counts from your arrival to the country not from when you were granted your current visa). You do not have to be a permanent resident to enrol to vote. 

You also must not be subject to sections 15 or 16 of the Immigration Act, for example have a conviction for certain offenses.
children.vote: You can cast a vote during the [[advance-voting]] period or cast an [[election-day-vote]].

children.title: I need help with English
children.question: Can I take someone in to help me vote if I don't speak English?
children.enrol: Enrolment information is available in several different languages and accessible formats to help guide you. The enrolment form itself is in English, if you require help with this you are able to ask someone around you for help to complete it.
children.vote: You are allowed to take a support person into the voting booth to help you translate, read and/or mark the voting papers. This can be a friend, family member or you may ask an electoral official to help you. They can go behind the voting screen with you to help, but they may not instruct you on who to vote for.

children.title: I am an Australian citizen residing in New Zealand
children.question: I am an Australian citizen who has lived in New Zealand for 3 years, can I vote?
children.enrol: You can enrol and vote once you have lived in New Zealand continuously for 12 months or more. You can enrol online using a **New Zealand passport** or *New Zealand drivers licence* or a **verified Realme login**, if you do not have these, you can complete a paper form.
children.vote: You can cast a vote during the [[advance-voting]] period or cast an [[election-day-vote]].

children.title: I am from the realm countries e.g. Niue, Cook Islands, or Tokelau
children.question: I am from Niue, Cook Islands or Tokelau and I don't know if I can enrol and vote in New Zealand
children.enrol: You can enrol and vote once you have lived in New Zealand continuously for 12 months or more. If you have not been to New Zealand for over 12 months you cannot vote. You can enrol online using a **New Zealand passport** or **New Zealand drivers licence** or a **verified Realme login**, if you do not have these, you can complete a paper form.
children.vote: You can cast a vote during the [[advance-voting]] period or cast an [[election-day-vote]]; or a [[special-vote]] (if you are not currently in NZ).

children.title: Trying to help someone else enrol and vote
children.description: There are a number of barriers or issues that can get between people and enrolling and voting - which of these apply?

children.title: Working or child care gets in the way of voting
children.description: Working or child care gets in the way

children.title: They have to take their kids with them
children.question: My neighbour has young children and they have no one to watch them while they vote. Can they take their children with them when they vote?
children.vote: The law requires a person to enter the voting booth alone, which is intended to protect the secrecy of their vote. However, in practice, voters may take their children into the voting booth with them if they cannot be left unattended.

children.title: They are an essential worker / working on election day
children.question: My daughter is an essential worker who is working on election day, what are the rules on being able to leave work to vote?
children.vote:
Voters are legally entitled to time away from work to vote on election day. They can also vote early at an [[advance-voting]] place. 

If they have not had a reasonable opportunity to vote before starting work on election day, and they are not required to carry out essential work or services, their employer must allow them to leave work to vote by 3pm. They are entitled to remain away from work for the rest of the day if necessary to vote, and their employer cannot deduct pay for the time off they take to vote. 

If they are required to work after 3pm to carry out essential work or services, their employer must allow them a reasonable amount of time earlier in the day to vote. Their employer cannot deduct pay for this time, provided they do not take more than two hours off work.

children.title: They are living somewhere temporarily for work e.g. seasonal workers, sharemilkers, away at training
children.question: My husband is doing seasonal farming work during the election period. Can he still vote while he is away from his usual address?
children.enrol: They can enrol online or by completing a paper form. Their residential address for enrolment purposes does not change if they are temporarily away from their usual home.
children.vote: If they are away from their usual place of residence, they can vote at the nearest voting place. As their name will not appear on the printed electoral roll at that location, they will need to complete a special declaration vote form before voting. This is known as a [[special-vote]].
source: Electoral Act s 61(b), s 72(6)(a), and s 162.

children.title: They are a shift worker
children.question: My wife works night shifts and sleeps during the day, how can she cast her vote?
children.vote: They can either vote during the [[advance-voting]] period or cast a [[takeaway-vote]].

children.title: I can't physically get to a polling place
They will be/are currently in hospital
children.question: My mum has to get surgery on the Friday before polling day, how can she vote?
children.enrol: They can enrol online or by completing a paper form, and they can have someone support them with the process if needed. Their enrolment address should be their usual residential address, not the hospital where they will be staying.
children.vote:
If they cannot get to a voting place because they are in hospital, they can authorise a friend or family member to collect their voting papers and bring the papers to them so they can cast a [[takeaway-vote]]. 

If they are scheduled to go into hospital before election day, it is best to vote in advance if they can. [[Advance-voting]] begins on **26 October**, 12 days before election day.

children.title: They can't leave care/ or the house
children.question: My son has health issues and doesn't like being in public, crowded, spaces. Can he still vote?
children.vote:
They can authorise someone to collect their voting papers from a voting place on their behalf - this process is known as a [[takeaway-vote]]. 

If they cannot get to a voting place and do not have someone who can collect their voting papers for them, they can contact their electorate manager. It may be possible for their voting papers to be delivered to them and then collected once they have completed them.

children.title: They are on home detention
children.question: My partner is serving a 6 month home detention sentence, can they still enrol to vote?
children.enrol: If they are on home detention, they can still enrol to vote, provided they meet the general eligibility criteria. They can enrol online or by completing a paper form.
children.vote: They can vote if they are on home detention or serving a community-based sentence. Election officials will provide their local probation services office with information about the voting options available to them.

children.title: They are in a rest home
children.question: My grandparents live in a residential care facility, I live far away and won't be able to help them enrol and vote, how can they enrol and vote on their own?
children.vote: If they are in a rest home and they won’t be able to go to a voting place, they don’t need to contact the Electoral Commission. Their local electorate manager will contact the manager of their care home to arrange voting services.

children.title: They have a physical disability
children.question: I work with a client who has lost a lot of their motor functions, including the use of their hands… can they vote? How can they seek assistance to vote?
children.enrol:
They can ask someone, such as a friend or family member, to support them in completing their enrolment form or to complete it on their behalf. 

A person who is enrolled to vote can complete and sign the form for them, and someone with power of attorney can also complete and sign it on their behalf. They can enrol online, or upload, email or post a completed form.
children.vote:
They can authorise someone to collect their voting papers from a voting place and bring the papers to them - this process is known as a [[takeaway-vote]].  

If they cannot get to a voting place and do not have someone who can collect their voting papers, they can contact their electorate manager. It may be possible for their voting papers to be delivered to them and then collected once they have completed them. 

They can also cast a vote at an [[advance-voting]] place and take a support person with them, including behind the voting screen if they would like.
source: Electoral Act s 170, s 167(2A), and s 85.

children.title: Names and identity
They have no ID
children.question: My teenage son doesn't have a license, passport, or kiwi access card, can he still enrol and vote without any of these?
children.enrol:
To enrol *online*, they'll need a **New Zealand drivers licence**, **New Zealand passport**, or a **verified RealMe identity**. 

If they do not have any of these, they can still enrol by completing an enrolment form online and having it emailed to themselves to sign, then uploading, emailing or posting the completed form. 

Alternatively, they can print a form themselves or request one to be sent to them, then return it by upload, email or post. Printed enrolment forms may also be available at selected public libraries, Electoral Commission offices, and potentially local post offices. They can contact their local library or post office for more information.
children.vote: They do not need to take any form of ID to vote. They can simply turn up to a voting place. They can take their EasyVote card to make the process quicker, but if they do not have one, that is okay too. Their details can be confirmed at the voting place.

children.title: They are gender diverse and have changed their name
children.question: My friend's prefered name differs from their legal name, and it has not been legally changed from their birth name. They are concerned about being questioned in public when they go to vote. What can they do?
children.enrol:
While the Electoral Act requires a voter's 'full' name to be used for voting and enrolment purposes, the Electoral Comissions does allow preferred names to be used (this does not have to match a legal record). 

If they are already enrolled but would like to change their enrolment details to match their preferred name, and this name vastly differs from the name that they are currently enrolled under, they should include their previously enrolled name when they are updating their details e.g., (previously enrolled as *Full name*) - this is to avoid potential issues regarding duplicate records. 

Please note, they may be limited when trying to use the online enrolment service, as it uses the details from their New Zealand passport, drivers licence or verified RealMe identity. If their preferred name does not match these records, they may need to complete a paper enrolment form instead and then upload, email or post it to the Electoral Commission. They may be contacted by the Electoral Comission to double check these details.
children.vote: They can vote using their preferred name if they were able to update their details before the enrolment due date on **25 October**.

children.title: They have made a change to their legal name e.g. through marriage, divorce, adoption, or reclaiming an ingoa Māori
children.question: My daughter no longer identifies with her ex-husbands surname. Can she vote with her maiden name, despite not legally changing her name on her ID?
children.enrol:
While the Electoral Act requires a voter's 'full' name to be used for voting and enrolment purposes, the Electoral Comissions does allow preferred names to be used (this does not have to match a legal record). 

If they are already enrolled but would like to change their enrolment details to match their preferred name, and this name vastly differs from the name that they are currently enrolled under, they should include their previously enrolled name when they are updating their details e.g., (previously enrolled as *Full name*) - this is to avoid potential issues regarding duplicate records. 

Please note, they may be limited when trying to use the online enrolment service, as it uses the details from their New Zealand passport, drivers licence or verified RealMe identity. If their preferred name does not match these records, they may need to complete a paper enrolment form instead and then upload, email or post it to the Electoral Commission. They may be contacted by the Electoral Comission to double check these details.
children.vote: They can vote using their preferred name if they were able to update their details before the enrolment due date on **25 October**.

children.title: Age
They are 17 but will turn 18 on or before the election day
children.question: My child is currently 17 years old and won't turn 18 until the day before election. Can they still enrol to vote?
children.enrol: Anyone can complete an enrolment form when they are 17. Then on their 18th birthday, they will be automatically enrolled and able to vote.
children.vote: If they turn 18 on election day, they can still vote as normal, provided they enrolled beforehand. If they enrolled **before 4 October**, they can cast an [[election-day-vote]]. If they enrolled **after 4 October but before 25 October**, they will cast a [[special-vote]] at the voting place.

children.title: I don't have a normal, fixed address
They live in a remote area
children.question: My co-worker will be in a remote area during the election with no voting places near them, how can they cast a vote?
children.vote:
They can authorise someone to collect their voting papers from a voting place on their behalf. If they cannot get to a voting place and do not have someone who can collect their voting papers, contact their electorate manager. 

Their electorate manager may be able to arrange for their voting papers to be delivered to them and then collected once they have completed them. If they are in a remote location within Aotearoa New Zealand, they may also be able to cast a [[special-vote]], if voting at a polling place would not be practicable without causing hardship or serious inconvenience. 

If they are unable to reach a voting place because they are in a remote location—for example, on a remote island administered by the Department of Conservation, at an offshore installation, or working on a vessel during the voting period—the Electoral Commission has a separate process for arranging voting services. For more information, call 0800 36 76 56.

children.title: They work at sea
children.question: My sister works on a cruise ship and will be working away from port during election time, how can she enrol and vote?
children.enrol: Their residential address for enrolment purposes does not change if they are temporarily absent from it.
children.vote:
If they are working on a ship that is in port and they are enrolled, or eligible to enrol, in the electorate where the ship is located, the ship’s master must allow them to go ashore to vote. If the ship will not be in port, or will not return to port, during the voting period, they may be eligible for a [[special-vote]]. 

For help with enrolling and voting, contact the Electoral Commission closer to election time on 0800 36 76 56 or at <enquiries@elections.govt.nz>.

children.title: They live on a boat
children.question: For the past few years, my dad has been living full-time on a boat. Can he enrol to vote?
children.enrol:
If someone's home is on a ship or boat that is permanently moored in a harbour, they should use the address of the ship or boat as their residential address. If their home is on a travelling ship or boat, they can use the last New Zealand address where they lived for at least 1 month, even if this was some time ago. 

They can then provide a postal address where they can receive mail, such as a PO Box or the address of a friend, family member, church or support group.

children.title: They do not have stable housing or a normal address
children.question: Some of my clients are experiencing homelessness/are unhoused and do no have an address to enrol, how can they still complete an enrolment form?
children.enrol:
They can enrol at a place where they spend a lot of time, or use their last residential address where they lived for at least 1 month, even if this was some time ago. 

If they do not feel safe receiving mail at this address, they can provide a different *postal* address where they can safely receive correspondence, such as the address of a friend, family member, church or support group.
children.vote:
The Electoral Commission lists all voting places online, so they can find one near them, or they can call 0800 36 76 56 for assistance. Voting places are often located at community hubs. 

To vote, they can simply go to a voting place during the [[advance-voting]] period from **26 October to 6 October** or on election day on **7 October**. The voting team will support them through the process, and they do not need to bring any form of ID.

children.title: They live overseas and do not have a New Zealand address
children.question: My mate is a kiwi who has recently moved overseas and doesn't have a New Zealand address, can they still vote?
children.enrol:
If they are a New Zealand citizen who has lived in New Zealand continuously for more than 12 months at some point in their life and have been back to New Zealand within the last 3 years, they are still eligible to enrol to vote. 

Not having a current New Zealand address does not prevent anyone from enrolling. Their electorate will be based on the last New Zealand address where they lived for at least **1 month**, and they can use an overseas address as their *postal* address to receive correspondence. 

They can enrol online using a **New Zealand passport**, **New Zealand drivers licence** or **verified RealMe identity**. If they do not have any of these, they can enrol using a paper form.
children.vote:
If they are overseas, they can download their voting papers from the Electoral Commission’s website, complete them and upload them online (they cannot return voting papers by email).

A link to download their voting papers will be available when overseas voting opens on **21 October**. They can complete the papers digitally or by hand. If completing them by hand, they can scan and upload them online, or post or hand-deliver them to an overseas voting place. 

If uploading their voting papers, they must be received by **7pm (NZ time)** on election day, which is **7 November**. 

They may also be able to vote in person at an overseas voting place. A list of overseas voting places will be available on the Electoral Commission’s website before the election.

children.title: Enrolment issues
They have been placed on the dormant roll
children.question: My mum hasn't voted in a while. She tried to enrol but found she had been placed on the dormant roll. How can she vote?
children.enrol:
To come off the [[dormant-roll]], they simply need to update their enrolment address. They must do this before voting starts on **26 October 2026**, as they cannot update their enrolment details at a voting place. 

To check or update their enrolment details, they can visit vote.nz or call 0800 36 76 56.
children.vote:
If they update their enrolment address before enrolment closes, they can vote normally. 

If they do not update their address **before midnight on 25 October** and have been on the dormant roll for less than 3 years, they can still vote. 

If their current address is in the same electorate as their previous enrolment address, they can cast both a party vote and an electorate vote. However, if their current address is in a different electorate, they can only cast a party vote.

children.title: Their enrolment details have changed
children.question: My brother has moved address recently, how can he change his enrolment information?
children.enrol:
They can enrol, check or update their details online at vote.nz using their **New Zealand drivers licence**, **New Zealand passport** or **verified RealMe identity**. 

They can also call 0800 36 76 56 to request an enrolment form, or they can free-text their name and address to 3676 to have a form sent to them. 

If voters provide their email address, phone number and postal address to the Electoral Commission, this will help them keep people updated about enrolment and voting.

children.title: They want to be on the unpublished roll
children.question: My daughter is worried that her abusive ex partner will find her new confidential address if she enrols to vote. Can she enrol to vote without her information becoming publicly accessible?
children.enrol:
They can apply to be on the [[unpublished-roll]], which means their details will not appear on publicly available printed electoral rolls. 

To apply, they can download and complete an application form and email it to the Electoral Commission, or they can call 0800 36 76 56 to have a form sent to them by post. 

They will need to provide evidence explaining why they need to be on the unpublished roll, such as a letter from their employer, lawyer, social worker, advocate or another person of standing in the community explaining why their circumstances place them at risk. 

They can also provide documents such as a current protection order under the Family Violence Act 2018 or a restraining order under the Harassment Act 1997.
children.vote: They can vote at any voting place in a general election, referendum or by-election. They will need to cast a [[special-vote]] because their details will not appear on the printed electoral roll used to issue voting papers at the voting place.

children.title: Health and disability
They will be/are currently in the hospital
children.question: My mum has to get surgery on the Friday before polling day, how can she vote?
children.enrol: They can enrol online or by completing a paper form, and they can have someone support them with the process if needed. Their enrolment address should be their usual residential address, not the hospital where they will be staying.
children.vote:
If they cannot get to a voting place because they are in hospital, they can authorise a friend or family member to collect their voting papers and bring the papers to them so they can cast a [[takeaway-vote]]. 

If they are scheduled to go into hospital before election day, it is best to vote in advance if they can. [[Advance-voting]] begins on **26 October**, 12 days before election day.

children.title: They are sectioned under the Mental Health Act
children.question: My sister has been detained in a hospital or secure facility for more than 3 years, can she still enrol and vote?
children.enrol:
If someone has been detained in a hospital or secure facility for 3 years or less, they can enrol and vote, as long as they meet the general eligibility requirements for enrolment.

If they've been detained in a hospital or secure facility, or they're subject to a compulsory treatment order, for more than 3 years, under:

- Section 24, or section 31 or section 33 of the Criminal Procedure (Mentally Impaired Persons) Act 2003, or under the corresponding provisions of the Criminal Justice Act 1985 (having been found unfit to stand trial or acquitted on account of insanity)
- Section 34 of the Criminal Procedure (Mentally Impaired Persons) Act 2003 or section 118 of the Criminal Justice Act 1985 (following conviction for an offence)
- Section 45(2) of the Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992 (the Mental Health Act), or section 29(1) of the Intellectual Disability (Compulsory Care and Rehabilitation) Act 2003 (for treatment of persons otherwise detained in prison because of their mental health or intellectual disability)

then they are *ineligible* to enrol and vote while they're detained.

The Director of Mental Health (or their delegate) is required to inform the Electoral Commission of any person detained in a hospital or secure facility who is, or becomes, ineligible to vote. The Electoral Commission will then remove them from the electoral roll.

When a person detained in a hospital or secure facility has been transferred from a prison or is released from the facility (as long as they are not released to prison), the Director of Mental Health is required to provide them with the opportunity to enrol to vote, if they are eligible. If they choose to exercise that opportunity, the Director of Mental Health must pass their enrolment information to the Electoral Commission.
children.vote:
If they have been detained for 3 years or less as at election day, they can enrol to vote if they also meet the general eligibility requirements. 

If they are eligible to vote from their facility, they’ll be able to participate in the 2026 General Election if they choose to. The Electoral Commission will work with their facility to provide them with voting services.
source:
- Section 24, or section 31 or section 33 of the Criminal Procedure (Mentally Impaired Persons) Act 2003, or under the corresponding provisions of the Criminal Justice Act 1985 (having been found unfit to stand trial or acquitted on account of insanity)
- Section 34 of the Criminal Procedure (Mentally Impaired Persons) Act 2003 or section 118 of the Criminal Justice Act 1985 (following conviction for an offence)
- Section 45(2) of the Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992 (the Mental Health Act), or section 29(1) of the Intellectual Disability (Compulsory Care and Rehabilitation) Act 2003 (for treatment of persons otherwise detained in prison because of their mental health or intellectual disability)
then you are *ineligible* to enrol and vote while you’re detained.

children.title: They are blind or have low vision
children.question: My neighbour is partially blind and needs help reading and marking the paper to vote, how can they receive help?
children.enrol:
A support person can help them enrol online or via paper form if they're blind or have low vision. 

If they can't sign the form, a support person can complete the form on their behalf.
children.vote:
Anyone may bring a support person to assist them to help them vote, read out the voting paper, and mark the paper for them if necessary. 

Furthermore, a telephone dictation voting service is available for blind and vision-impaired voters and voters who have a physical disability that prevents them from marking the voting paper independently and in secret. 

They need to register to use this service, even if they've used it at previous elections.

**Registration** for the telephone dictation service opens on **Monday 5 October 2026**, and will close at **noon** (NZT) on election day, **Saturday 7 November 2026**.

**Voting** with the telephone dictation service opens on **Wednesday 21 October 2026**, and will close at **7pm** (NZT) on election day, **Saturday 7 November 2026**.

children.title: They have a physical disability
children.question: I work with a client who has lost a lot of their motor functions, including the use of their hands… can they vote? How can they seek assistance to vote?
children.enrol:
They can ask someone, such as a friend or family member, to support them in completing their enrolment form or to complete it on their behalf. 

A person who is enrolled to vote can complete and sign the form for them, and someone with power of attorney can also complete and sign it on their behalf. 

They can enrol online, or upload, email or post a completed form.
children.vote:
They can authorise someone to collect their voting papers from a voting place and bring the papers to them - this process is known as a [[takeaway-vote]].  

If they cannot get to a voting place and do not have someone who can collect their voting papers, they can contact their electorate manager. It may be possible for their voting papers to be delivered to them and then collected once they have completed them. 

They can also cast a vote at an [[advance-voting]] place and take a support person with them, including behind the voting screen if they would like.
source: Electoral Act s 170, s 167(2A), and s 85.

children.title: They have a mental health issue
children.question: My nephew struggles with severe anxiety and we don't know if he can vote on his own, how can he get help to enrol and vote?
children.enrol:
They can ask a support person to help them enrol online if they wish. 

A support person can also complete and sign an enrolment form on their behalf if they require help because of a mental impairment. 

To *sign* the enrolment form on someone elses behalf, the support person must be enrolled to vote; have enduring power of attorney; or be the person’s appointed welfare guardian. If required, the support person can also fill in another form so the Electoral Commission can contact them as the voter's representative.
children.vote:
If they need help with voting, a friend, family member or electoral official can be their support person and assist them.

Their support person can:

- Go behind the voting screen with them
- Read out the words and information on their voting paper
- Mark the voting papers for them if they ask them to.
- Their support person can't tell them who they should vote for. 

They can vote as long as they want to and can clearly indicate their voting choice. However, they must be present and able to indicate their choice at the time the vote is cast. If they're not able to do this, no one can cast a vote on their behalf, even someone with power of attorney or guardianship.

children.title: They have dementia
children.question: My grandparent has dementia, can they still vote?
children.enrol:
A support person can help someone with dementia to enrol to vote. A support person can also complete and sign an enrolment form on their behalf if they require help. 

To *sign* the enrolment form on their behalf, the support person must be enrolled to vote; have enduring power of attorney; or be the person’s appointed welfare guardian. 

If someone is helping a person with dementia enrol, they will need to fill in another form so the Electoral Commission can contact them as their representative. They can ring 0800 36 76 56 for the form.
children.vote:
People living with dementia, or any other cognitive impairment, are able to continue to vote if they wish to do so. They can have help voting by taking a support person with them to the voting place.

A person with dementia can vote as long as they want to and can clearly indicate their voting choice. However, they must be present and able to indicate their choice at the time the vote is cast. If they're not able to do this, no one can cast a vote on their behalf, even someone with power of attorney or guardianship.

children.title: They need help marking the paper
children.question: My aunty struggles with gripping pens/pencils to write and needs help marking the voting papers
children.vote:
Anyone may bring a support person to assist them to vote, read out the voting paper, and mark the paper for them if necessary. 

The support person cannot tell them who to vote for.

children.title: Prison, remand, home detention etc
They are on home detention
children.question: My partner is serving a 6 month home detention sentence, can they still enrol to vote?
children.enrol: If you are on home detention, you can still enrol to vote, provided you meet the general eligibility criteria. You can enrol online or by completing a paper form.
children.vote: You can vote if you are on home detention or serving a community-based sentence. Election officials will provide your local Probation Services office with information about the voting options available to you.

children.title: They are in prison
children.question: My dad is currently serving a prison sentence of 2 years, can he still vote and will he be able to vote from prison?
children.enrol: You can still enrol, but this depends on when the offences you were sentenced for occured. If the offences you were sentenced for were before 20 December 2025 and your sentence is under 3 years, you can enrol and vote. Prison staff assist those who are eligible and enrolment applications are individually scanned and emailed to the Electoral Commission.
children.vote:
This depends on when the offences you were sentenced for occured. If the offences you were sentenced for were before 20 December 2025 and your sentence is under 3 years, you can vote. 

During the [[advance-voting]] period, mobile voting teams will attend prisons and set up voting facilities for prisoners who are eligible to vote.

children.title: They are on remand
children.question: My client is in prison while on remand waiting for his trial, can he still enrol to vote?
children.enrol: If you're on remand, you can still enrol to vote if you meet the general eligibility criteria. You do not face the same restrictions as those who have been sentenced. If you are in prison while on remand, prison staff will assist those who are eligible and enrolment applications are individually scanned and emailed to the Electoral Commission.
children.vote: If you're in a police cell in the electorate on election day, a voting team may visit before midday so you can vote. If you are in prison while on remand, during the [[advance-voting]] period, mobile voting teams will attend prisons and set up voting facilities for those who are eligible to vote.

children.title: They are on community service
children.question: My cousin is serving a community service sentence, can they still vote?
children.enrol: If you're serving a community based sentence, you can still enrol to vote. You can do this online or via paper form.
children.vote: You can vote if you're on home detention or serving a community-based sentence. Election officials will give your local Probation Services information about the voting options available to you.

children.title: Overseas voters
They are living overseas
children.question: My niece is living or staying in Australia at the time of the election, can she still enrol and vote and how can she do it?
children.enrol:
If you are a New Zealand citizen, who has lived in New Zealand for more than 12 months continuously at some point in your life **AND** have been to New Zealand in the last 3 years - you are still eligible to enrol to vote. Your electorate will be where you last lived in New Zealand for longer than 1 month and you may set your postal address to your overseas address to ensure you receive correspondence. 

You can enrol online using a **New Zealand passport** or a **New Zealand drivers licence** or a **verified Realme login**. If you don't have either of these, you can also enrol via paper form.
children.vote:
You can cast a [[special-vote]].

The best way to vote from overseas is to download your voting papers from the electoral commission's website, complete them, then upload them online (you cannot send back voting papers through email). 

A link to download your voting papers will be available on the electoral commission's website from the date overseas voting opens on **21 October**. You can complete the papers both digitally (marking the paper digitally) or physically, if you choose to complete them by hand you can scan and upload them online, or you can post or hand deliver them to your nearest overseas voting place. 

If you're uploading your voting papers, you must return them by **7pm (NZ time)** on election day which is **7 November**.

You may also be able to vote at an overseas voting place. A list of overseas voting places will be available on the electoral commission's website prior to the election.

children.title: They are overseas as a member of the military or diplomatic service
children.question: My wife is a member of the New Zealand Defence Force and stationed overseas, can she still enrol to vote?
children.enrol:
You can enrol and vote no matter how long you've been outside of New Zealand if you are one of the following: public servant working overseas and their families; New Zealand diplomats or trade representatives and their families; members of the New Zealand Defence Force and their families. 

You can enrol online using a **New Zealand passport** or a **New Zealand drivers licence** or a **verified Realme login**. If you don't have either of these, you can also enrol via paper form.

children.title: They are a seasonal worker or temporarily living overseas for work
children.question: I am living somewhere temporarily for work for a few months, how do I vote?
children.enrol:
You can still enrol and vote if you are a New Zealand citizen or resident for electoral purposes and only residing outside of New Zealand temporarily for work (if you have been back to New Zealand in the last 3 years). Your residential address for enrolment purposes does not change because you are temporarily absent from it. 

You can enrol online using a **New Zealand passport** or a **New Zealand drivers licence** or a **verified Realme login**. If you don't have either of these, you can also enrol via paper form.

children.title: Migrant in NZ, residents & language
They have migrated to New Zealand / They are a resident or visa holder
children.question: My uncle is a migrant in NZ who has been here for 2 years and he has never voted before, is he able to vote?
children.enrol:
You can enrol to vote as a migrant, resident or visa holder **IF** you have a visa that does not require you to leave within a specified time **AND** you must have lived in New Zealand continuously for 12 months or more (this generally counts from your arrival to the country not from when you were granted your current visa). You do not have to be a permanent resident to enrol to vote. 

You also must not be subject to sections 15 or 16 of the Immigration Act, for example have a conviction for certain offenses.
children.vote: You can cast a vote during the [[advance-voting]] period or cast an [[election-day-vote]].

children.title: They need help with English
children.question: My grandma can't speak English, can she take someone in to help her vote?
children.enrol: Enrolment information is available in several different languages and accessible formats to help guide you. The enrolment form itself is in English, if you require help with this you are able to ask someone around you for help to complete it.
children.vote: You are allowed to take a support person into the voting booth to help you translate, read and/or mark the voting papers. This can be a friend, family member or you may ask an electoral official to help you. They can go behind the voting screen with you to help, but they may not instruct you on who to vote for.

children.title: They are an Australian citizen residing in New Zealand
children.question: My flatmates are Australian citizens who have lived in New Zealand for 3 years, can they vote?
children.enrol: You can enrol and vote once you have lived in New Zealand continuously for 12 months or more. You can enrol online using a **New Zealand passport** or *New Zealand drivers licence* or a **verified Realme login**, if you do not have these, you can complete a paper form.
children.vote: You can cast a vote during the [[advance-voting]] period or cast an [[election-day-vote]].

children.title: They are from the realm countries e.g. Niue, Cook Islands, or Tokelau
children.question: My friend is from Niue, Cook Islands or Tokelau and they don't know if they can enrol and vote in New Zealand
children.enrol: You can enrol and vote once you have lived in New Zealand continuously for 12 months or more. If you have not been to New Zealand for over 12 months you cannot vote. You can enrol online using a **New Zealand passport** or **New Zealand drivers licence** or a **verified Realme login**, if you do not have these, you can complete a paper form.
children.vote: You can cast a vote during the [[advance-voting]] period or cast an [[election-day-vote]]; or a [[special-vote]] (if you are not currently in NZ).
